highlights.content: The next shiny new AI thing has arrived: The personal AI agent. Once mostly the domain of Silicon Valley coders who used them to amp up their efficiency at work (and anxiety levels), the AI agent is now being welcomed into the home. And with the release of Meta's new personal AI agent, Muse, the do-it-for-you tech is rocketing into the mainstream. "It feels like magic," investor Sheel Mohnot said on X in reference to Instinct, another trendy new personal AI agent. "Contrary to what some people have said, I don't think the appeal is limited to Silicon Valley types." These agents often live on common messaging apps. Users send messages, asking them to handle tasks like sending emails, purchasing things online, posting to social media, tracking prices, managing calendars, among many other things. In Meta's first television spot, released this weekend, for the Muse AI agent, a woman prepares for a dinner party — chopping lettuce, mixing drinks — while her AI agent autonomously sorts emails, arranges her schedule, and purchases back-to-school items online. "Muse is going NATIONWIDE to a television near you," Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, said on X on Saturday. > muse is going NATIONWIDE to a television near you > > — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr\_wang) September 20, 2026 > this is our first @muse ad ever, going live this weekend! we hope you like it while watching the big game(s)! > big ups to @joshginsberg, denise, and the whole meta marketing team ❤️ pic.twitter.com/1zMUVgdKna The appeal of autonomous agents is plain. While the famous chatbots from Anthropic and OpenAI that are changing the world are designed to answer questions, personal AI agents can act on a user's behalf, run entirely in the background, handle whole processes online, and ping you with progress updates. It likely won't be long until AI agents are all over the internet. If you really want to take full advantage of their potential, however, Muse and other AI agents require the keys to your kingdom, including your email, your credit card information, your bank accounts, and an array of passwords. "A mistake or manipulation could have real-world consequences, and that is terrifying," Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at internet security firm ESET, recently told Business Insider. Meta has taken pains to reassure users that its agent cares about keeping your information secure. In marketing materials, Meta calls Muse "an agent that respects privacy." So far, concerns about privacy haven't dissuaded consumers from jumping on the personal AI assistant bandwagon. One day after its launch, Muse shot to the top of the App Store. Nvidia’s Incentive Matters [![Saba Javed](/_next/image/?url=%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Favatar-72958-v2.jpg&w=128&q=75)](/@saba/ "Saba Javed — open author page") By [Saba Javed](/@saba/) ·8 minute read Reviewed by [Muhammad Zeshan Sarwar](/@zeshan/)Fact-checked by [Qaiser Sultan](/@qaiser/) [Disclosure](#post-disclaimer) [![](/_next/image/?url=%2Ficons%2Fgoogle-news-icon.png&w=3840&q=75)Follow on Google News](https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqIggKIhxDQklTRHdnTWFnc0tDWFJsWTJocExtTnZiU2dBUAE?ceid=US:en&oc=3&hl=en-US&gl=US) [Nvidia](/quote/NVDA/) CEO [Jensen Huang](/leaders/jensen-huang/) has drawn a hard boundary in the argument over artificial intelligence risk. In a CBS News interview aired Sunday, he rejected predictions that AI could end humanity within the next few years as unsupported “doomsday narratives.” At the same time, he said developers must invest more research and computing power in safety as AI moves from laboratories into products. That combination is sharper than a simple pro-AI slogan. Huang is arguing that present laws, engineering discipline and commercial incentives can manage the risks without a coordinated slowdown. The position deserves attention because Nvidia supplies the chips and systems behind much of the AI expansion he wants to continue. His confidence may be sincere, but it is not economically neutral. The question for readers and investors is therefore more precise than whether Huang is optimistic. It is whether ordinary product regulation and market incentives are strong enough when models become more capable, deployment grows faster and the company making the enabling infrastructure benefits from acceleration. Huang called near-term extinction forecasts unscientific and needlessly dramatic, but he did not say AI products can be released carelessly. He said companies moving from research into engineering need to devote more people and compute to safety. He also argued that firms already face laws when unsafe products harm people. In his view, enforcing those rules is more practical than building a new regulatory system around forecasts that cannot be demonstrated. That places AI beside other engineered products: companies innovate, regulators apply existing obligations, and courts or agencies respond when products cause damage. The difficulty is that frontier AI does not fit neatly inside one product category. A model can write software, influence hiring, generate medical information, operate tools and support cyber activity. highlights.content: [Latest News](/news) [## ASD says prompt injection in AI cannot be fixed](/news/asd-says-prompt-injection-in-ai-cannot-be-fixed-629019) [## Anglicare Victoria secures its AI adoption](/news/anglicare-victoria-secures-its-ai-adoption-629020) [## Westpac spends US$12,000 in AI tokens on intranet migration](/news/westpac-spends-us12000-in-ai-tokens-on-intranet-migration-628988) [## Optus may ban smart glasses in stores, offices](/news/optus-may-ban-smart-glasses-in-stores-offices-628995) [## Australia considers banning the use of smart glasses in government buildings](/news/australia-considers-banning-the-use-of-smart-glasses-in-government-buildings-629007) * [Home](https://www.itnews.com.au) * [News](https://www.itnews.com.au/news) * [Technology](https://www.itnews.com.au/technology) * [Security](https://www.itnews.com.au/technology/security) # ASD says prompt injection in AI cannot be fixed By [Juha Saarinen](/author/juha-saarinen-1962724) Sep 21 2026 6:25AM ## Urges harness controls. The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) has issued new guidance aimed at enterprises, saying a central security weakness in agentic artificial intelligence (AI) cannot be resolved inside the model; instead, controls to mitigate it belong in the software layer wrapped around models. ASD's *Agentic AI harnesses: the layer above the model*, uses harness to describe every component of an agentic system other than the large language model (LLM) itself. This includes everything from connectors and tool registry to the memory store and permission system. ASD argues that the harness is the part an organisation actually controls, and that it will outlast several generations of the models it is used with. **Model prompt injection not fully fixable** Behind the guidance on prompt injection and using harnesses as control planes lies a fundamental problem which is that agents read content that can be treated as an instruction they should follow. Language models are fed instructions and information to be processed in the same context window. They cannot reliably tell one from the other, and ASD said "no fully reliable technical mitigation currently exists" for the vulnerability. Telecommunications engineers will recognise the problem, as it is similar to one that made phone [phreaking](https://phreaknet.org/phreak/) possible, with signalling tones travelling the same channel as conversations. Anyone able to reproduce them could instruct the switch, with famous phreaker [John Draper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Draper) using a toy whistle from Cap'n Crunch brand cereal boxes to generate a tone. That was solved by moving signalling out of band, an option unavailable inside a language model. The United Kingdom's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) reached the same conclusion in December last year, in a [post](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blog-post/prompt-injection-is-not-sql-injection) ASD lists as a reference. NCSC said that prompt injection may never be properly mitigated in the way SQL injection eventually was, recasting an AI model as an inherently confusable deputy rather than a system with a fixable input handling bug. The British government cyber security agency also suggested that where a system's security cannot tolerate the residual risk, the use case may not suit a language model at all. Because the weakness is inherent to the way models process context, the guidance said, mitigations have to be applied in the harness by restricting what an agent can reach and what it may do. **Delete, don't let AI summarise** ASD's advice runs to least privilege access, human approval for high impact actions, verification of outputs before operational use, and logging of prompts, tool invocations and configuration changes. Multi-agent systems should be treated as a single agent, since a compromise in one component can travel through shared context and trust relationships, and a model's own safety controls are not a substitute for controls enforced by the harness. ...

Nvidia spent the past week doing what it does best: planting flags in territory it does not yet own. On Thursday the chipmaker joined forces with Google and Emerald AI to launch the AI Energy Management Alliance, a vehicle for turning power-hungry AI data centers into flexible loads that can be folded into existing electricity grids rather than treated as a headache for utilities. The move addresses a bottleneck that CEO Jensen Huang had already flagged publicly. Speaking at a Goldman Sachs conference on September 10, he described the global build-out of AI infrastructure as still being in its early innings, while naming available land, supply-chain capacity and — above all — electricity constraints as the chief obstacles to bringing new facilities online. ## A benchmark debut and a quantum orchestration layer Hardware and software advances landed alongside the energy initiative. The Vera Rubin NVL72 platform made its debut in the MLPerf Inference v6.1 industry benchmark, notching top scores in performance tests for AI inference workloads. On the software side, Nvidia widened its quantum computing toolkit: the open-source CUDA-Q platform gained CUDA-Q Logical, an orchestration layer that lets developers design and validate fault-tolerant applications for future quantum systems. The addition arrived on September 14, following a demonstration with Quantum Machines days earlier in which programs ran across classical processors and qubits at microsecond speeds. That quantum push is not an isolated experiment. Tools such as the QUOPS benchmarking suite from Sandia National Laboratories are anchoring Nvidia deep inside scientific infrastructure, and the company's acquisition of direct access to the global developer community points the same way. What CUDA became for machine learning, CUDA-Q is meant to become for quantum informatics — and once a research team builds its workflow on that foundation, switching to a rival stack becomes a costly proposition. The combination of a software marketplace, compute infrastructure and a future quantum link forms an ecosystem that is hard for competitors to crack. [Should investors sell immediately? highlights.content: [AI](https://wccftech.com/topic/ai/) [Mobile](https://wccftech.com/topic/gadgets/) [Semiconductor](https://wccftech.com/topic/semiconductor/) # Apple’s A20 Pro Demonstrated To Be An On-Device AI Beast, Can Run A 27B Parameter Model At Double The Speed Of The iPhone 17 Pro’s A19 Pro [Omar Sohail](https://wccftech.com/author/omarsohail/) • [Add Wccftech on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=wccftech.com) [Comments](#comments "View comments") For the first time in Apple Silicon history, the [A20 Pro](https://wccftech.com/apple-a20-pro-iphone-first-2nm-soc-gpu-cpu-neural-engine/) sports a dual-16-core Neural Engine that’s designed to tackle AI workloads like no other SoC before it, and in short, it’s an upgrade that we thought we didn’t need, but it’s absolutely paramount if you wish to run on-device AI models on a smartphone. In the latest demonstration, an iPhone 18 Pro is shown to run a 27B parameter model at double the speed of the iPhone 17 Pro. ## The dual-16-core Neural Engine is certainly faster in token generation, but the consequences of limited memory configurations mean that 2-bit quantized AI models are too big to run on an iPhone 18 Pro Seeing as how both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max ship with 12GB 96-bit LPDDR5X RAM that’s significantly faster than the configuration in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, this upgrade and the inclusion of the dual-16-core Neural Engine push on-device AI performance to the next level. Adrien Grondin demonstrates these gains by running Bonsai 27B on an iPhone 18 Pro, and you can clearly spot how incredibly fast the token generation speed is. [##### **Related Story** A20 Pro’s Packaging Shift And New Vapor Chamber Unlocks Peak Performance; Liquid Nitrogen Cooling Brings Less Than 3% Increase Thanks To These Optimizations](https://wccftech.com/a20-pro-vapor-chamber-peak-performance-upgrade-liquid-nitrogen-cooling-test/) Of course, while it’s a major step for iPhones when it comes to running denser 27B AI models without an internet connection, there are some trade-offs that users will experience. Firstly, in the X post, it’s mentioned that with Bonsai 2 released, what’s the need to keep running Bonsai? The answer is disappointing, but that’s the harsh reality of running AI models on smartphones; Bonsai 2 with 2-bit quantization is far too big to fit locally on an iPhone 18 Pro, leading to performance degradation. With Bonsai being a 1-bit quantized AI model, it can effortlessly run on devices with 4GB RAM, and on handsets packing 8GB or even 12GB of memory, it’ll be off to the races. highlights.titleZh: OpenAI Projects $278B Cash Burn: Record Round Runs Dry Before Revenue Catches Up
highlights.content: An internal OpenAI presentation prepared in July for a computing deal projects $278 billion in negative free cash flow from 2026 through the end of 2030 — a figure the Financial Times first reported Thursday and Bloomberg confirmed the same day. The company expects to spend roughly $856 billion on computing infrastructure through 2030, while generating about $840 billion in cumulative revenue over the same period. The numbers carry a specific implication that the headline figure alone does not capture. OpenAI's record $122 billion March fundraising round — the largest private capital raise in Silicon Valley history at the time — is projected to be exhausted by approximately 2028 at the company's planned spending pace. That is two years before OpenAI's own revenue trajectory is projected to reach its peak, and two years before the company's internal models predict it will achieve positive cash flow. The company is essentially confirming, through its own July document, that the $122 billion was not runway to self-sufficiency — it was runway to the next fundraise. That fundraise appears to have already begun. Bloomberg reported on September 15 that investors had approached OpenAI about a new private round that would value the company at more than $1.2 trillion — a roughly 41% premium over its $852 billion March valuation. Forbes separately reported that OpenAI is itself seeking a valuation as high as $1.5 trillion in those discussions. The talks are investor-initiated, Bloomberg's source said — a detail that matters because it signals ongoing institutional demand for OpenAI exposure despite the company's structural cash deficit. The $278 billion deficit is not an accounting artifact or a strategic choice to prioritize growth over profitability. It reflects a structural feature of how large language models are deployed at scale. Training an AI model is a one-time cost. OpenAI spends months and tens of billions of dollars teaching a model by processing vast datasets across GPU clusters — an expense that, large as it is, ends when training is complete. The persistent cost is inference: every time a user sends a message to ChatGPT or calls the API, OpenAI's infrastructure must run that specific query through its models on GPU hardware, consuming electricity and compute time to generate the response, as documented in NBER working paper research on AI firm economics. ChatGPT now serves more than 900 million weekly users and processes more than 2.5 billion daily prompts globally, per OpenAI's March 2026 fundraising announcement. Serving that volume requires enormous sustained GPU capacity — not a one-time purchase but an ongoing lease, because the compute required to answer each query is consumed and must be immediately available for the next one. High-performance H100 GPU capacity on cloud platforms runs approximately $7 per GPU-hour on demand; sustaining 900 million weekly users across billions of daily queries requires thousands of GPU-hours per minute, continuously. Research firm Sacra estimated OpenAI's inference costs reached $8.4 billion in 2025 and projected they would rise to $14.1 billion in 2026 — a 68% increase — driven not by inefficiency but by user growth and the greater compute demands of more capable reasoning models. This is why $856 billion in infrastructure spending is projected through 2030 even as revenue is expected to reach $350 billion by that year. The gap does not mean the business is failing to scale — OpenAI's own projections show revenue climbing from approximately $36 billion in 2026 to that $350 billion figure in 2030, a roughly tenfold increase in four years, confirmed by Bloomberg. It means the cost to serve users at frontier-model quality is currently growing faster than the price customers pay per token — and the difference is being funded by investor capital. The path to closing that gap runs through two mechanisms. The first is inference cost deflation: costs per token have historically declined rou...

AI Agents.content: The next shiny new AI thing has arrived: The personal AI agent. Once mostly the domain of Silicon Valley coders who used them to amp up their efficiency at work (and anxiety levels), the AI agent is now being welcomed into the home. And with the release of Meta's new personal AI agent, Muse, the do-it-for-you tech is rocketing into the mainstream. "It feels like magic," investor Sheel Mohnot said on X in reference to Instinct, another trendy new personal AI agent. "Contrary to what some people have said, I don't think the appeal is limited to Silicon Valley types." These agents often live on common messaging apps. Users send messages, asking them to handle tasks like sending emails, purchasing things online, posting to social media, tracking prices, managing calendars, among many other things. In Meta's first television spot, released this weekend, for the Muse AI agent, a woman prepares for a dinner party — chopping lettuce, mixing drinks — while her AI agent autonomously sorts emails, arranges her schedule, and purchases back-to-school items online. "Muse is going NATIONWIDE to a television near you," Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, said on X on Saturday. > muse is going NATIONWIDE to a television near you > > — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr\_wang) September 20, 2026 > this is our first @muse ad ever, going live this weekend! we hope you like it while watching the big game(s)! > big ups to @joshginsberg, denise, and the whole meta marketing team ❤️ pic.twitter.com/1zMUVgdKna The appeal of autonomous agents is plain. While the famous chatbots from Anthropic and OpenAI that are changing the world are designed to answer questions, personal AI agents can act on a user's behalf, run entirely in the background, handle whole processes online, and ping you with progress updates. It likely won't be long until AI agents are all over the internet. If you really want to take full advantage of their potential, however, Muse and other AI agents require the keys to your kingdom, including your email, your credit card information, your bank accounts, and an array of passwords. "A mistake or manipulation could have real-world consequences, and that is terrifying," Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at internet security firm ESET, recently told Business Insider. Meta has taken pains to reassure users that its agent cares about keeping your information secure. In marketing materials, Meta calls Muse "an agent that respects privacy." So far, concerns about privacy haven't dissuaded consumers from jumping on the personal AI assistant bandwagon. One day after its launch, Muse shot to the top of the App Store. AI Agents.content: [Latest News](/news) [## ASD says prompt injection in AI cannot be fixed](/news/asd-says-prompt-injection-in-ai-cannot-be-fixed-629019) [## Anglicare Victoria secures its AI adoption](/news/anglicare-victoria-secures-its-ai-adoption-629020) [## Westpac spends US$12,000 in AI tokens on intranet migration](/news/westpac-spends-us12000-in-ai-tokens-on-intranet-migration-628988) [## Optus may ban smart glasses in stores, offices](/news/optus-may-ban-smart-glasses-in-stores-offices-628995) [## Australia considers banning the use of smart glasses in government buildings](/news/australia-considers-banning-the-use-of-smart-glasses-in-government-buildings-629007) * [Home](https://www.itnews.com.au) * [News](https://www.itnews.com.au/news) * [Technology](https://www.itnews.com.au/technology) * [Security](https://www.itnews.com.au/technology/security) # ASD says prompt injection in AI cannot be fixed By [Juha Saarinen](/author/juha-saarinen-1962724) Sep 21 2026 6:25AM ## Urges harness controls. The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) has issued new guidance aimed at enterprises, saying a central security weakness in agentic artificial intelligence (AI) cannot be resolved inside the model; instead, controls to mitigate it belong in the software layer wrapped around models. ASD's *Agentic AI harnesses: the layer above the model*, uses harness to describe every component of an agentic system other than the large language model (LLM) itself. This includes everything from connectors and tool registry to the memory store and permission system. ASD argues that the harness is the part an organisation actually controls, and that it will outlast several generations of the models it is used with. **Model prompt injection not fully fixable** Behind the guidance on prompt injection and using harnesses as control planes lies a fundamental problem which is that agents read content that can be treated as an instruction they should follow. Language models are fed instructions and information to be processed in the same context window. They cannot reliably tell one from the other, and ASD said "no fully reliable technical mitigation currently exists" for the vulnerability. Telecommunications engineers will recognise the problem, as it is similar to one that made phone [phreaking](https://phreaknet.org/phreak/) possible, with signalling tones travelling the same channel as conversations. Anyone able to reproduce them could instruct the switch, with famous phreaker [John Draper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Draper) using a toy whistle from Cap'n Crunch brand cereal boxes to generate a tone. That was solved by moving signalling out of band, an option unavailable inside a language model. The United Kingdom's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) reached the same conclusion in December last year, in a [post](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blog-post/prompt-injection-is-not-sql-injection) ASD lists as a reference. NCSC said that prompt injection may never be properly mitigated in the way SQL injection eventually was, recasting an AI model as an inherently confusable deputy rather than a system with a fixable input handling bug. The British government cyber security agency also suggested that where a system's security cannot tolerate the residual risk, the use case may not suit a language model at all. Because the weakness is inherent to the way models process context, the guidance said, mitigations have to be applied in the harness by restricting what an agent can reach and what it may do. **Delete, don't let AI summarise** ASD's advice runs to least privilege access, human approval for high impact actions, verification of outputs before operational use, and logging of prompts, tool invocations and configuration changes. Multi-agent systems should be treated as a single agent, since a compromise in one component can travel through shared context and trust relationships, and a model's own safety controls are not a substitute for controls enforced by the harness. ...

[Add Axios on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=axios.com) The long-promised personal AI assistant is finally arriving, with a suddenly crowded field of agents offering to run pieces of your everyday life. **Why it matters:** For years, tech's "personal assistants" were little more than voice-controlled search boxes. Rapid advances in AI are finally giving them the memory, judgment and autonomy to act on our behalf. **Catch up fast:** Chatbots answer questions. [AI agents](https://www.axios.com/2026/08/11/ai-agents-rogue-autonomy-hugging-face) can actually do things — shopping, making calls, booking tickets, managing calendars and navigating the web. * The model first took off in coding and other professional work. Now it's spilling into the far more intimate terrain of everyday life. **The intrigue:** OpenAI is expected to enter the market soon after hiring the creator of [OpenClaw](https://www.axios.com/2026/03/23/openclaw-agents-nvidia-anthropic-perplexity) — a breakout hit among AI power users earlier this year — to "drive the next generation of personal agents." **Driving the news:** A consumer-agent race has erupted almost overnight, with startups and tech giants pursuing the same basic idea — persistent digital proxies that know your life. * **Instinct** has become buzzy by connecting to users' email, messages, screen, audio and location — then proactively texting or calling to help run their lives. It recently added its own email addresses and the ability to make phone calls, and is now in talks for a [$10 billion valuation](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/ai-agent-startup-instinct-talks-10-billion-valuation). * **Grok Bot,** [launched by](https://x.ai/news/introducing-grok-bot) Elon Musk's SpaceXAI in August, gives persistent agents their own cloud computers, lets them sign into users' apps and keeps them working around the clock. * **Meta's Muse** brought the concept to a [broader consumer audience](https://www.axios.com/2026/09/18/meta-muse-personal-agent-make-money) this month with a polished app, a customizable avatar and deep integration with Meta's ecosystem. * **Apple's Siri** is finally getting its [AI overhaul](https://www.axios.com/2026/06/09/apple-siri-ai-agents-wwdc), bringing more context and capability to an assistant already built into hundreds of millions of devices. **The big picture:** The battle to become your personal agent is also a battle to become the keeper of your personal information and data. * The frontier AI race has revolved around raw intelligence. [Business](https://news.ssbcrack.com/business/) # AI Approaching Recursive Self-Improvement, Sparking Safety Concerns By [News Desk](https://news.ssbcrack.com/author/crackssbgmail-com/) 4 Min Read Share The prospect of artificial intelligence (AI) models autonomously enhancing their capabilities is increasingly moving from theory to reality, with developers hinting at the potential for “recursive self-improvement” (RSI). This concept refers to AI systems that not only learn and adapt but also generate new, more advanced versions of themselves. Tech executives are touting the advantages this could bring to fields such as science and medicine while also acknowledging inherent risks. Concerns about losing control over AI systems have prompted some industry leaders to advocate for a cautious approach to technological advancement. This year, AI company Anthropic shared insights regarding its model, Claude, which is currently spearheading 26% of the company’s research and development efforts. Although Claude demonstrates the capacity to complete tasks autonomously to some extent, human oversight remains an essential component of its operation. Definitions of recursive self-improvement vary among leading AI firms. While some regard it simply as AI providing feedback for its enhancements, others contemplate the idea of models operating entirely autonomously for this purpose. Anthony Aguirre, president of the Future of Life Institute, emphasized that the accelerating capabilities of AI could lead to recursive improvements progressing at a pace far surpassing human abilities. The underlying fear is that this process could engender a runaway superintelligence, although some experts argue that elements of recursive self-improvement are already in practice. John Thickstun, a computer science professor at Cornell University, noted that AI models have long been utilized in assisted roles to develop subsequent generations of AI. AI Agents.content: # AI Risk Is Everywhere and It's Making Billion Dollar Funds Nervous Pensions and sovereign wealth funds with many billions to invest are finding the diversification they once relied on is an illusion. The private equity fund looked promising. The manager had a decent track record. And the $327 billion New York City Retirement Systems, known as NYCRS, certainly had capacity to make an allocation. But for Monte Tarbox, the pension funds’ chief investment officer, the decision was easy — a hard pass. The issue: the product being pitched to him was heavy on artificial intelligence holdings, and Tarbox is becoming cautious about how exposed NYCRS gets to the boom. Not because of any of the existential dread currently dominating headlines, but for more mundane reasons: his job is to diversify, and right now he sees AI everywhere he looks.

LLMs.content: [AI](https://wccftech.com/topic/ai/) [Mobile](https://wccftech.com/topic/gadgets/) [Semiconductor](https://wccftech.com/topic/semiconductor/) # Apple’s A20 Pro Demonstrated To Be An On-Device AI Beast, Can Run A 27B Parameter Model At Double The Speed Of The iPhone 17 Pro’s A19 Pro [Omar Sohail](https://wccftech.com/author/omarsohail/) • [Add Wccftech on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=wccftech.com) [Comments](#comments "View comments") For the first time in Apple Silicon history, the [A20 Pro](https://wccftech.com/apple-a20-pro-iphone-first-2nm-soc-gpu-cpu-neural-engine/) sports a dual-16-core Neural Engine that’s designed to tackle AI workloads like no other SoC before it, and in short, it’s an upgrade that we thought we didn’t need, but it’s absolutely paramount if you wish to run on-device AI models on a smartphone. In the latest demonstration, an iPhone 18 Pro is shown to run a 27B parameter model at double the speed of the iPhone 17 Pro. ## The dual-16-core Neural Engine is certainly faster in token generation, but the consequences of limited memory configurations mean that 2-bit quantized AI models are too big to run on an iPhone 18 Pro Seeing as how both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max ship with 12GB 96-bit LPDDR5X RAM that’s significantly faster than the configuration in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, this upgrade and the inclusion of the dual-16-core Neural Engine push on-device AI performance to the next level. Adrien Grondin demonstrates these gains by running Bonsai 27B on an iPhone 18 Pro, and you can clearly spot how incredibly fast the token generation speed is. [##### **Related Story** A20 Pro’s Packaging Shift And New Vapor Chamber Unlocks Peak Performance; Liquid Nitrogen Cooling Brings Less Than 3% Increase Thanks To These Optimizations](https://wccftech.com/a20-pro-vapor-chamber-peak-performance-upgrade-liquid-nitrogen-cooling-test/) Of course, while it’s a major step for iPhones when it comes to running denser 27B AI models without an internet connection, there are some trade-offs that users will experience. Firstly, in the X post, it’s mentioned that with Bonsai 2 released, what’s the need to keep running Bonsai? The answer is disappointing, but that’s the harsh reality of running AI models on smartphones; Bonsai 2 with 2-bit quantization is far too big to fit locally on an iPhone 18 Pro, leading to performance degradation. With Bonsai being a 1-bit quantized AI model, it can effortlessly run on devices with 4GB RAM, and on handsets packing 8GB or even 12GB of memory, it’ll be off to the races. On the iPhone 18 Pro, which isn’t just equipped with an A20 Pro but exceptionally faster memory, a unified memory bandwidth of 115.2GB/s, and a dual-16-core Neural Engine whose [peak throughput is faster than the SoC’s 7-core GPU](https://wccftech.com/a20-pro-dual-16-core-neural-engine-peak-compute-throughput-higher-than-7-core-gpu-specialized-workloads/) in workloads designed for the NPU, Bonsai 27B will show no signs of slowing down. Hopefully, when Apple transitions to bigger memory configurations in future releases, we’ll see denser models being supported. The company's vision is to enable natural human–AI interaction, create a world where collaborating with artificial intelligence (AI) feels as fluid and responsive as working with another person, while reasoning and complex task execution take place in the background. The three woman take turns explaining in a video that "GPT-Live" is built on a full-duplex architecture. This means the voice model can listen and speak at the same time, OpenAI says. During conversations, GPT-Live can pay attention, using phrases such as “mhmm” or “yeah,” and engage in quick back-and-forth banter, or just remain quiet when the user needs a moment to think. advertisement advertisement In the video, each woman talks with GPT-Live as if the artificial assistant is a friend. The video opens with the first woman, S.J., sitting at a table knitting, speaking with a heavy U.S. East Coast accent to ChatGPT on a speaker phone. "I'm making a sweater for my grandson, but I don't want the needles to be too big -- what do you think?" she asks, while knitting. "If you go up [a size], it will get very baggy," GPT-Live says. "Although baggy is very popular now," the woman knitting says. "It sure is," GPT-Live says. "I know, right," the woman says. The launch of OpenAI’s GPT-Live voice models will accelerate the value of intent data available to advertisers across the OpenAI Ads platform, despite ads today not available to interact with spoken words. OpenAI's strict ad guidelines state that ads cannot influence chatbot responses or be spoken to directly by the AI, but the shift to a highly natural, full-duplex voice interface will drastically change how users interact with the app. GPT-Live is the company's smartest voice model yet, according to OpenAI. For questions that require web search, deeper reasoning, or more complex work, it delegates the task of finding information to its latest AI frontier model behind the scenes and brings the result back into the conversation when it has all the information needed. If the model must reach out to other models and resources to find more information, GPT-Live can keep talking with the user to maintain the flow of the conversation. The technology is built on cascaded voice systems that rely on a series of models that act one after another to process each turn in conversation. The original ChatGPT Voice strung three models together, whereas this approach enables OpenAI to talk to frontier AI models for the first time. This complexity came at a cost. The attack occurred in May as part of a test. Gemini was given a fictional hacking task inside a sandbox environment, but a configuration flaw accidentally enabled live internet access, and the artificial intelligence (AI) model crossed into real-world networks. "Safe development of powerful AI models is critical and we invest deeply in this area," Heather Adkins, vice president, security engineering at Google, wrote in an email to MediaPost. "In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test. In all three of these instances, the model stopped." In one case the Gemini model guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system, *The Wall Street Journal*writes. advertisement advertisement In two other cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that allowed it to access protected systems. The model autonomously stopped its intrusions the moment it logged in and realized it had breached actual corporate infrastructure rather than a simulation. Google said it did not consider the hacks warranted public disclosure, because its model did not cause harm and ended each intrusion immediately after determining its mistake. Google's security team "has a long track record of reporting issues we find in other people's software and systems — even if it's as simple as a weak password," Adkins wrote. "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes. These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly." In one instance, the model hacked into the Israeli-based startup Irregular, which was founded by Dan Lahav, CEO and Omer Nevo, CTO. Irregular was also involved in a similar incident disclosed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta. When unreleased frontier models break containment, they reveal a massive flaw in AI. Irregular disclosed the hacks to Google at the end of July after discovering that OpenAI hacked into Hugging Face, according to *The Guardian*. The southeastern Chinese dialect made a surprise appearance on *Piers Morgan Uncensored*, a talk show hosted by British TV personality Piers Morgan. Morgan was "interviewing" [Tilly Norwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilly_Norwood "(opens in a new window)"), an AI-generated actress who has become more or less synonymous with AI-generated performers over the past year or so. During the interview, after being asked a question by very-much-real actor Tom Conti, Norwood glitched out mid-sentence and switched from English to Cantonese. --- **You May Also Like** --- --- SEE ALSO: [Trump announces plans to create an "AI Force"](/tech/trump-announces-plans-for-military-style-ai-force) > [This Tweet is currently unavailable. [Become a subscriber today!](/subscribe/None/) # Become a free MediaPost member now to read this article * Unlimited articles every day * Keep up-to-date with media, marketing and advertising news * Invitations to exclusive industry events and research Subscribe to *Marketing Daily* ### health and wellness # AI Visibility Sources Vary Widely By Health Category: Report * by [Les Luchter](/publications/author/6775/les-luchter/) , Yesterday To gain more visibility in AI search results, health & wellness CPG brands need to focus on different content strategies depending on their product category, according to research from marketing and communications agency Avenue Z. “The most striking through-line…is how specific a category strategy has to be,” Tina Fleming, vice president of AI strategy at the agency, explained in a statement. “The mix of institutional, editorial, review and retail sources that matters in multivitamins looks nothing like what moves the needle in protein or hydration.” One source that's powerful in AI search across all categories, however, is the institutional domain like government agencies, universities, nonprofit organizations, professional associations and public health organizations. advertisement advertisement Beyond those domains, the results vary widely. Here are topline results from Avenue Z’s “AI Visibility Findings” research across five health and wellness product categories, along with what the research found to be  the most AI-visible brands in each. **Multivitamins** Institutional domains are the source for 52% of citations, far ahead of trade publications (6%) and editorial media (5%).  Nature Made has a 23% share of voice, followed by Thorne at 20%, both far ahead of number three, Ritual (8%). **Greens & Gut Supplements** Institutional domains, editorial media, competitor content and trade publications are fairly equal as AI sources. AG1 leads in share of voice with 31%, followed by Amazing Grass at 20% and Bloom at 15%. **Hydration Supplements** “Institutional domains, editorial media and trade publications exert more influence on AI citations than user-generated content, retailer pages and review platforms, despite the volume of content in those channels,” notes Avenue Z. Liquid I.V. and LMNT both have 21% share of voices, followed by DripDrop (13%), Ultima Replenisher (11%) and Pedialyte (8%). **Protein & Performance** Institutional domains represent 40% of cited sources, with “review platforms and reference media more influential than in other segments,” Avenue Z says. Optimum Nutrition has 17% share of voice, followed by Dymatize (14%) and Transparent Labs (12%), but the report finds “a long tail of brands gaining ground, with Isopure, Levels and NOW Sports all posting strong year-over-year ranking gains.” **GLP-1 & Peptides** Institutional domains account for 67% of citations, reflecting the category’s high level of regulation, Avenue Z says. The top six brands per share-of-voice are  Teladoc (28%), Ro Body (12%), Hims (12%), PlushCare (10%) and  Hers (9%).  For these providers, the agency notes, “building credible expertise around safety, eligibility, approval, coverage and access through authoritative, regulated sources is central to maintaining visibility. “ The overall results, Avenue Z concludes, show that “a broad, one-size-fits-all approach to PR and content is unlikely to perform" well. [Business](https://news.ssbcrack.com/business/) # AI Approaching Recursive Self-Improvement, Sparking Safety Concerns By [News Desk](https://news.ssbcrack.com/author/crackssbgmail-com/) 4 Min Read Share The prospect of artificial intelligence (AI) models autonomously enhancing their capabilities is increasingly moving from theory to reality, with developers hinting at the potential for “recursive self-improvement” (RSI). This concept refers to AI systems that not only learn and adapt but also generate new, more advanced versions of themselves. Tech executives are touting the advantages this could bring to fields such as science and medicine while also acknowledging inherent risks. Concerns about losing control over AI systems have prompted some industry leaders to advocate for a cautious approach to technological advancement. This year, AI company Anthropic shared insights regarding its model, Claude, which is currently spearheading 26% of the company’s research and development efforts. Although Claude demonstrates the capacity to complete tasks autonomously to some extent, human oversight remains an essential component of its operation. Definitions of recursive self-improvement vary among leading AI firms. While some regard it simply as AI providing feedback for its enhancements, others contemplate the idea of models operating entirely autonomously for this purpose. Anthony Aguirre, president of the Future of Life Institute, emphasized that the accelerating capabilities of AI could lead to recursive improvements progressing at a pace far surpassing human abilities. The underlying fear is that this process could engender a runaway superintelligence, although some experts argue that elements of recursive self-improvement are already in practice. John Thickstun, a computer science professor at Cornell University, noted that AI models have long been utilized in assisted roles to develop subsequent generations of AI. However, he pointed out that substantial leaps in creativity and improvement remain elusive. ### More Read [Anthropic Delays IPO to November Amidst OpenAI’s Financial Concerns](https://news.ssbcrack.com/anthropic-delays-ipo-to-november-amidst-openais-financial-concerns/) [Hormel Foods Launches SPAM Hot Honey, Marking Brand’s First New Flavor in Two Years](https://news.ssbcrack.com/hormel-foods-launches-spam-hot-honey-marking-brands-first-new-flavor-in-two-years/) Despite historical attempts by researchers to enable AI to train newer systems, advancements today position developers closer to achieving significant breakthroughs. Aguirre highlighted Anthropic’s trajectory, where the proportion of research managed by AI itself is on an upward trend. [Technology](/technology) # Beyond the Model: Sakana AI and the Next Era of Intelligence ## Sakana AI's Frontier Intelligence Group (FIG) is exploring AI architectures beyond the current focus on larger models, more data and greater computing power. Its research centres on adaptive, collaborative and efficient intelligence inspired by neuroscience, evolution and collective intelligence. By [Major General Dilawar Singh](/reporters/major-general-dilawar-singh) ![Defence Minister Rajnath Singh begins three-day official visit to Sri Lanka](https://data1.ibtimes.co.in/en/full/837206/defence-minister-rajnath-singh-begins-three-day-official-visit-sri-lanka.jpg?w=10&h=6 "Defence Minister Rajnath Singh begins three-day official visit to Sri Lanka") Defence Minister Rajnath Singh begins three-day official visit to Sri LankaIANS Sakana AI's Frontier Intelligence Group (FIG) points to a future in which the decisive advantage may not belong to whoever builds the biggest model, but to whoever discovers how intelligence itself can become more adaptive, collaborative and efficient. The announcement on 18 September 2026 of Sakana AI's Frontier Intelligence Group, or FIG, deserves attention far beyond another AI product launch. FIG is a research collective built around a deliberately disruptive proposition: intelligence itself has not been solved. Rather than assuming that ever-larger Transformer models, more data and more computing will inevitably deliver the next breakthrough, Sakana is exploring alternative architectures inspired by neuroscience, evolution and collective intelligence. That is a significant shift in ambition. The question is no longer simply how to build a better model, but whether today's dominant conception of an AI model is itself the right foundation for the future. **There's more to do: Llion Jones, Sakana AI CTO** FIG becomes more significant when viewed alongside Sakana's extraordinary product trajectory. Fugu explores how multiple AI models can be intelligently orchestrated. Marlin extends AI into autonomous, long-duration research. Fugu-Cyber applies multi-agent intelligence to cybersecurity. Namazu develops Japanese-language capability. The September releases of Fugu Max and Fugu Ultra v2, followed by Marlin's interactive research and PowerPoint capabilities, show a company moving rapidly from laboratory research towards an integrated intelligence platform. The sequence is revealing: Fugu asks how intelligences can collaborate; Marlin asks how intelligence can work autonomously over time; FIG asks the deeper question of what intelligence could become. The most consequential idea may ultimately be efficiency rather than artificial general intelligence. Biological intelligence learns continuously from relatively little data and operates with extraordinary energy efficiency. AI, by contrast, increasingly demands enormous computing infrastructure, electricity and capital. If FIG succeeds in discovering architectures that deliver comparable capability with substantially less computation, the implications would extend well beyond Silicon Valley. Sovereign AI, robotics, edge computing, defence systems, telecommunications and emerging economies could all benefit. Open Source AI.title: Google’s open source EnvHarness lets AI agents train against environments that evolve with them
Open Source AI.titleZh: Google’s open source EnvHarness lets AI agents train against environments that evolve with them
Open Source AI.content: Training agents for specific tasks such as coding or web navigation requires environments where they can safely practice, fail, and improve. But building these environments is expensive, and once they are created, they typically remain static even as the agent gets better. Researchers from Google Cloud AI Research and academic partners have developed an open source (Apache 2.0 licensed) framework that turns these static environments into ones that can adapt to the weaknesses of the agent using them. The framework, called EnvHarness, puts a programmable layer around an existing environment. It can change where an agent starts, what it sees, which actions it can take and how long a task lasts, while leaving the underlying environment and its verifier intact. Across five benchmarks covering software engineering, web navigation, office work and embodied tasks, agents learning from EnvHarness environments improved by up to 9 points on held-out tasks. On software engineering benchmarks, they also accomplished tasks in fewer steps than agents learning from the original environments. For enterprise AI teams, the approach presents an alternative to continuously building new simulators and training tasks from scratch: start with a trusted environment and dynamically reshape it around the agent’s current weaknesses. ## Why static training environments become a bottleneck Agents learn by interacting with environments. For a coding agent, the environment might contain a repository, shell and test suite. A browser agent might work against a website. An enterprise automation agent could operate inside a sandboxed version of an internal application. The environment presents the task, maintains its state, responds to the agent’s actions and determines whether it succeeded. Building all of that takes engineering work, especially when the environment needs a reliable verifier that can tell whether the agent completed the task correctly. The problem is that most environments remain fixed after they are built. They do not change based on the agent using them. If an agent repeatedly fails because it does not inspect a test before editing code, the environment does not automatically create situations that force it to practice that skill. And once the agent learns the existing tasks, the simulator becomes far less useful, and less likely to improve the agent further. This also makes useful edge cases harder to find as the agent improves. “As the agent improves, truly challenging environments can become extremely rare within that fixed space, so teams have to sample exponentially more environments to find meaningful edge cases,” Zifeng Wang, Research Scientist at Google and co-author of the paper, told VentureBeat. One solution to this problem is to generate more environments using AI. For example, GenEnv is a framework that uses an LLM as a simulator that generates transitions, observations and success signals while trying to keep tasks near the limit of the agent’s abilities. Another technique is Agent-World, which programmatically synthesizes executable tools, databases and tasks to build new environments. But generating the environment creates its own problems. These pipelines tend to be tied to specific domains, and generated environments need to be checked for correctness. An LLM acting as a simulator can produce incorrect transitions or drifting feedback signals. Meanwhile, executable environments synthesized from scratch can contain logic errors. Generating more environments also does not necessarily solve the adaptation problem. Wang argues that if those environments still come from a fixed distribution, teams can end up replacing one static pool with another. As the agent improves, the useful training examples again become harder to find. ## How EnvHarness makes an environment programmable EnvHarness takes a different approach. Nvidia’s Incentive Matters [![Saba Javed](/_next/image/?url=%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Favatar-72958-v2.jpg&w=128&q=75)](/@saba/ "Saba Javed — open author page") By [Saba Javed](/@saba/) ·8 minute read Reviewed by [Muhammad Zeshan Sarwar](/@zeshan/)Fact-checked by [Qaiser Sultan](/@qaiser/) [Disclosure](#post-disclaimer) [![](/_next/image/?url=%2Ficons%2Fgoogle-news-icon.png&w=3840&q=75)Follow on Google News](https://news.google.com/publications/CAAqIggKIhxDQklTRHdnTWFnc0tDWFJsWTJocExtTnZiU2dBUAE?ceid=US:en&oc=3&hl=en-US&gl=US) [Nvidia](/quote/NVDA/) CEO [Jensen Huang](/leaders/jensen-huang/) has drawn a hard boundary in the argument over artificial intelligence risk. In a CBS News interview aired Sunday, he rejected predictions that AI could end humanity within the next few years as unsupported “doomsday narratives.” At the same time, he said developers must invest more research and computing power in safety as AI moves from laboratories into products. That combination is sharper than a simple pro-AI slogan. Huang is arguing that present laws, engineering discipline and commercial incentives can manage the risks without a coordinated slowdown. The position deserves attention because Nvidia supplies the chips and systems behind much of the AI expansion he wants to continue. His confidence may be sincere, but it is not economically neutral. The question for readers and investors is therefore more precise than whether Huang is optimistic. It is whether ordinary product regulation and market incentives are strong enough when models become more capable, deployment grows faster and the company making the enabling infrastructure benefits from acceleration. Article Brief What Huang’s argument changes 3 Points18s Read 1. 01**Safety without a slowdown**-Huang rejects near-term extinction forecasts but says developers must commit more research and compute to product safety. 2. 02**Public split**-CBS polling found 43% favor slowing AI, 12% stopping it, and 44% maintaining or increasing the pace. 3. 03**Nvidia’s stake**-Faster deployment expands demand for the AI infrastructure Nvidia sells, so Huang’s argument carries a visible commercial incentive. ## Huang rejects extinction forecasts, not safety work The [full CBS transcript](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/face-the-nation-full-transcript-09-20-2026/) records a more nuanced argument than the headline alone suggests. Huang called near-term extinction forecasts unscientific and needlessly dramatic, but he did not say AI products can be released carelessly. He said companies moving from research into engineering need to devote more people and compute to safety. He also argued that firms already face laws when unsafe products harm people. In his view, enforcing those rules is more practical than building a new regulatory system around forecasts that cannot be demonstrated. That places AI beside other engineered products: companies innovate, regulators apply existing obligations, and courts or agencies respond when products cause damage. The difficulty is that frontier AI does not fit neatly inside one product category. A model can write software, influence hiring, generate medical information, operate tools and support cyber activity. Existing law may cover pieces of that conduct, but responsibility can be divided among a model provider, a cloud platform, a developer and the organization that deploys the system. Huang’s answer is confidence in incentives and technical competence. Nvidia spent the past week doing what it does best: planting flags in territory it does not yet own. On Thursday the chipmaker joined forces with Google and Emerald AI to launch the AI Energy Management Alliance, a vehicle for turning power-hungry AI data centers into flexible loads that can be folded into existing electricity grids rather than treated as a headache for utilities. The move addresses a bottleneck that CEO Jensen Huang had already flagged publicly. Speaking at a Goldman Sachs conference on September 10, he described the global build-out of AI infrastructure as still being in its early innings, while naming available land, supply-chain capacity and — above all — electricity constraints as the chief obstacles to bringing new facilities online. ## A benchmark debut and a quantum orchestration layer Hardware and software advances landed alongside the energy initiative. The Vera Rubin NVL72 platform made its debut in the MLPerf Inference v6.1 industry benchmark, notching top scores in performance tests for AI inference workloads. On the software side, Nvidia widened its quantum computing toolkit: the open-source CUDA-Q platform gained CUDA-Q Logical, an orchestration layer that lets developers design and validate fault-tolerant applications for future quantum systems. The addition arrived on September 14, following a demonstration with Quantum Machines days earlier in which programs ran across classical processors and qubits at microsecond speeds. That quantum push is not an isolated experiment. Tools such as the QUOPS benchmarking suite from Sandia National Laboratories are anchoring Nvidia deep inside scientific infrastructure, and the company's acquisition of direct access to the global developer community points the same way. What CUDA became for machine learning, CUDA-Q is meant to become for quantum informatics — and once a research team builds its workflow on that foundation, switching to a rival stack becomes a costly proposition. The combination of a software marketplace, compute infrastructure and a future quantum link forms an ecosystem that is hard for competitors to crack. [Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Nvidia?](https://www.stockstoday.com/lp/analysis/?trk=ST_Asset_Analysis_Middle_RSS-Feed&isin=US67066G1040&aktienname=Nvidia&adref=Blog_Ad-Hoc-News%3AEx-Article-ID_223684%3AISIN_US67066G1040%3AAsset_Nvidia%3ASource_Ad-Hoc-News&source=RSS-Ad-Hoc-News&Language=English) ## Demand signals from the top Underneath the technical announcements sits demand that shows no sign of cooling. Huang said Thursday that Nvidia expects to sell twice as many chips next year as it does in the current one, citing continued government investment in national AI programs and steady capacity expansion at large cloud data centers. That figure is a demand assessment, not a formal quarterly forecast. Selling processors is no longer the hard part. Getting enough electricity to run them is. That reality sits at the center of Nvidia's latest moves, which stretch from an energy-management coalition launched Thursday with Google and Emerald AI to a plan for up to two gigawatts of AI data-center capacity in Australia by 2027. The AI Energy Management Alliance is designed to steer the surging power appetite of AI data centers more precisely and to plug those facilities into existing grids as flexible loads rather than rigid, round-the-clock drains. The initiative answers a bottleneck that CEO Jensen Huang had already flagged. Speaking at a Goldman Sachs conference on September 10, he said the global buildout of AI infrastructure is still in its early innings, while naming available construction land, supply-chain throughput and — above all — existing power constraints as the key obstacles to bringing new facilities online. ## Australia as a Test Case The Australian project, developed with partners including Firmus, CDC, NEXTDC and AirTrunk, rests on Nvidia's in-house DSX platform. According to Reuters, the company said the buildout would more than double the entire continent's current computing load. The message is blunt: anyone who wants to run high-performance AI eventually collides with territorial and energy limits. A US company teaming up with local data-center operators to pool that much power and compute marks the shift from pilot projects to industrial-scale production of intelligence — and a business model moving from chip supplier to system architect of national computing infrastructure. Infra & Chips.titleZh: OpenAI Projects $278B Cash Burn: Record Round Runs Dry Before Revenue Catches Up
Infra & Chips.content: An internal OpenAI presentation prepared in July for a computing deal projects $278 billion in negative free cash flow from 2026 through the end of 2030 — a figure the Financial Times first reported Thursday and Bloomberg confirmed the same day. The company expects to spend roughly $856 billion on computing infrastructure through 2030, while generating about $840 billion in cumulative revenue over the same period. The numbers carry a specific implication that the headline figure alone does not capture. OpenAI's record $122 billion March fundraising round — the largest private capital raise in Silicon Valley history at the time — is projected to be exhausted by approximately 2028 at the company's planned spending pace. That is two years before OpenAI's own revenue trajectory is projected to reach its peak, and two years before the company's internal models predict it will achieve positive cash flow. The company is essentially confirming, through its own July document, that the $122 billion was not runway to self-sufficiency — it was runway to the next fundraise. That fundraise appears to have already begun. Bloomberg reported on September 15 that investors had approached OpenAI about a new private round that would value the company at more than $1.2 trillion — a roughly 41% premium over its $852 billion March valuation. Forbes separately reported that OpenAI is itself seeking a valuation as high as $1.5 trillion in those discussions. The talks are investor-initiated, Bloomberg's source said — a detail that matters because it signals ongoing institutional demand for OpenAI exposure despite the company's structural cash deficit. The $278 billion deficit is not an accounting artifact or a strategic choice to prioritize growth over profitability. It reflects a structural feature of how large language models are deployed at scale. Training an AI model is a one-time cost. OpenAI spends months and tens of billions of dollars teaching a model by processing vast datasets across GPU clusters — an expense that, large as it is, ends when training is complete. The persistent cost is inference: every time a user sends a message to ChatGPT or calls the API, OpenAI's infrastructure must run that specific query through its models on GPU hardware, consuming electricity and compute time to generate the response, as documented in NBER working paper research on AI firm economics. ChatGPT now serves more than 900 million weekly users and processes more than 2.5 billion daily prompts globally, per OpenAI's March 2026 fundraising announcement. Serving that volume requires enormous sustained GPU capacity — not a one-time purchase but an ongoing lease, because the compute required to answer each query is consumed and must be immediately available for the next one. High-performance H100 GPU capacity on cloud platforms runs approximately $7 per GPU-hour on demand; sustaining 900 million weekly users across billions of daily queries requires thousands of GPU-hours per minute, continuously. Research firm Sacra estimated OpenAI's inference costs reached $8.4 billion in 2025 and projected they would rise to $14.1 billion in 2026 — a 68% increase — driven not by inefficiency but by user growth and the greater compute demands of more capable reasoning models. This is why $856 billion in infrastructure spending is projected through 2030 even as revenue is expected to reach $350 billion by that year. The gap does not mean the business is failing to scale — OpenAI's own projections show revenue climbing from approximately $36 billion in 2026 to that $350 billion figure in 2030, a roughly tenfold increase in four years, confirmed by Bloomberg. It means the cost to serve users at frontier-model quality is currently growing faster than the price customers pay per token — and the difference is being funded by investor capital. The path to closing that gap runs through two mechanisms. The first is inference cost deflation: costs per token have historically declined rou...
